questions.text: The deck says 130,000 installations in 2 years, but your own releases say 100,000 and then 120,000, and only one French article says 'nearly 130,000'. How do you define an installation, and how many of those are active engines that actually send signals today?
questions.why: Installations are the top-of-funnel for the whole open-source-to-CTI monetization case, and the 130K figure sits at the top of the publicly reported range.
questions.evidence_to_request: Dated export of the installation/enrollment database (unique machine IDs) with monthly cumulative and 30-day active engines, plus the dedup methodology and the dashboard behind the Sept 2022 figure.

questions.text: The deck says you monetize CTI access for those not sharing, but what is actual paid conversion so far? How many of those 130K installs are paying, what is ARR, and what stops a non-sharer from just using the free tier or a fork given the MIT license?
questions.why: The business model rests on converting free users to paid CTI access, and no evidence has been shown that it works.
questions.evidence_to_request: Billing/Stripe export, current ARR and pipeline, pricing tiers, and conversion funnel from install to paid CTI subscriber.

questions.text: You claim 92% of bad traffic is blocked by IP reputation alone and that CTI is '99.99% sure' actionable. What dataset and methodology produced those numbers, and what is the measured false-positive rate?
questions.why: These product-efficacy claims underpin the core value proposition of the CTI offer, yet no method or source is provided.
questions.evidence_to_request: Methodology and raw data behind the 92%, 0.35% fire-list, and 99.99% figures, including false-positive rates, test environment and any third-party validation.

questions.text: The deck says 'we don't compete', yet CrowdSec sells its own WAF/IDS/IPS and is listed as a direct alternative to Fail2ban and Cloudflare WAF. Who do you displace in the budget, and how do incumbents respond when you encroach?
questions.why: Positioning as a complement affects market sizing and competitive risk, and the deck also overstates its G2 comparisons, such as only 3 startups in the top 50, which suggests loose framing.
questions.evidence_to_request: Competitive win/loss list, customer replacement examples, and a breakdown of which budget lines CrowdSec revenue displaces.

questions.text: You cite 3 exits and 4 fundraisers for the CEO, but we can only verify the 2016 NBS System sale. Can you walk us through each exit and raise, and also the G2 'leader in 30+ categories' claim when G2 lists you in only 6?
questions.why: Founder track record and third-party validation are credibility signals, and both are overstated relative to public sources.
questions.evidence_to_request: Founder CVs with company names, exit dates and acquirers, cap table or round history of prior ventures, and the G2 badge/category report.

title: CrowdSec Series A deck (2022)

brief.headline: Dig deeper: the whole case rests on 130,000 installations, which sits at the top of the press range, and the deck shows no revenue or paid conversion.
brief.summary: CrowdSec is an MIT-licensed open-source security engine that crowdsources IP reputation and plans to monetize threat-intelligence access for users who do not share signals. The deck claims 130,000 installations in 2 years, 7.2M bad IPs identified, 19M daily reports and a network spanning 175 countries. The network figures are supported or plausible, but they are dated and mostly come from company-issued sources. The 130,000 install count is unverified: the company's own releases say 100,000 and 120,000, and only one French article says nearly 130,000. Several secondary claims are overstated or contradicted: "we don't compete", "only 3 of 50 are startups" and "leader in 30+ categories". The CEO's 3 exits are also unconfirmed, with only one verified. None of these breaks the thesis alone, but together they show a habit of rounding up, and the monetization claim is untested.
strengths: Three co-founders confirmed by independent sources, each of whom previously ran a company; the CEO has been in cybersecurity since 1999.
Ranked #17 on G2's 2022 best security products list, confirmed by G2 and VentureBeat, ahead of GitHub, Symantec, Dynatrace and Tenable.

Network scale is credible: 7.2M bad IPs matches the 2021 Series A announcement, and the 175-country footprint matches the company's October 2022 press release, with later coverage citing 190+ countries.
Open-source distribution gives low-friction adoption and a data network effect, since more engines mean more signals.

red_flags.text: The central traction number, 130,000 installations in 2 years, is unverified and at the top of the 100K-130K range in press coverage. The company's own releases say 100K and 120K, and installations are not defined, so active engines sending signals are unknown.

The monetization model, selling CTI access to non-sharers, has no revenue, ARR or paid-conversion evidence. MIT licensing and a free tier make it unclear what stops non-sharers from forking or staying free.

The security-efficacy figures (92% of bad traffic blocked by IP reputation alone, 0.35% fire list, 99.99% actionable) have no stated methodology, dataset or false-positive rate, and none has been checked.

Competitive and ranking claims are overstated. "We don't compete" is contradicted, since CrowdSec sells its own WAF/IDS/IPS and is listed as an alternative to Fail2ban and Cloudflare WAF. "Only 3 of 50 are startups" is contradicted by at least five startups on the list. Microsoft outranks CrowdSec on the list, so "outranked Microsoft" holds only for GitHub.

Credential inflation: only one CEO exit (NBS System, 2016) is verified, versus 3 exits and 4 fundraisers claimed. "Leader in 30+ categories" looks like badge counting, since G2 lists CrowdSec in 6 categories.

questions: How do you define an installation, and how many of the 130K are active engines sending signals in the last 30 days today?
What is actual paid conversion for CTI access: how many paying customers, what ARR, and what stops a non-sharer from using the free tier or a fork under the MIT license?
What dataset and method produced the 92% blocked, 0.35% fire list and 99.99% actionable figures, and what is the measured false-positive rate?
You say you don't compete, but you sell a WAF/IDS/IPS and are listed against Fail2ban and Cloudflare WAF. Whose budget do you displace, and how do incumbents respond?
Can you walk us through each of the CEO's 3 exits and 4 raises, and explain the 30+ categories claim when G2 lists you in 6?
